sections.title: Detailed Brief Overview
rows: Concept Name
**Subject-Verb Agreement** (कर्त्ता-क्रिया संगति / Syntax)
Core Definition
A verb in a sentence must agree with its subject in **Number** (Singular/Plural) and **Person** (1st, 2nd, 3rd Person).
Fundamental Formula
**Singular Subject (SS) → Singular Verb (SV)** | **Plural Subject (PS) → Plural Verb (PV)**
Scope in UPSSSC PET
Core topic under **General English** syllabus; directly tested in **Spotting Errors**, **Fill in the Blanks**, and **Sentence Improvement**.
Primary Challenge
Identifying the **real subject** when separated from the verb by prepositional phrases, relative clauses, or compound conjunctions.
Singular Verbs List
**is, was, has, does, V1+s/es** (e.g., plays, writes, runs)
Plural Verbs List
**are, were, have, do, V1 (base form)** (e.g., play, write, run)
Verb vs Noun 'S' Rule
Adding **'s/es'** to a Noun makes it **Plural** (Boy → Boys), but adding **'s/es'** to a Verb makes it **Singular** (Play → Plays).
Weightage & Impact
Guaranteed 1–2 direct questions in UPSSSC PET English section; forms the basis of all grammatical error detection.

items.title: Rule 1: Compound Subjects with 'AND' & The 'Single Unit' Exception
items.content:
• **General Rule:** Two or more singular subjects joined by **'and'** take a **Plural Verb**.
• **Exception 1 (Single Idea/Unit):** If two nouns joined by 'and' express a **single idea**, form a **pair/food combination**, or refer to the **same person/thing**, use a **Singular Verb**.
• **Exception 2 (Single Person with One Article):** If two singular nouns joined by 'and' are preceded by an article or possessive adjective before the **first noun only**, they refer to the **same person** → **Singular Verb**.
• **Trick/Formula:** **[Article + Noun1 + and + Noun2 = Singular Person = SV]** vs **[Article + Noun1 + and + Article + Noun2 = Two Persons = PV]**
• **Example 1:** Incorrect: Rahul and Rohit **is** going to Lucknow. | **Correct:** Rahul and Rohit **are** going to Lucknow. (Two distinct persons)
• **Example 2:** Incorrect: Bread and butter **are** a wholesome breakfast. | **Correct:** Bread and butter **is** a wholesome breakfast. (Single meal unit)
• **Example 3:** Incorrect: Slow and steady **win** the race. | **Correct:** Slow and steady **wins** the race. (Single idea)
• **Example 4:** Incorrect: The Director and Producer **have** arrived. | **Correct:** The Director and Producer **has** arrived. (One person dual role - single article)
• **Example 5:** Incorrect: The Director and **the** Producer **has** arrived. | **Correct:** The Director and **the** Producer **have** arrived. (Two separate individuals - two articles)

items.title: Rule 2: Correlative Conjunctions & The Proximity Principle (समीपस्थता का नियम)
items.content:
• **General Rule:** When subjects are connected by **'Either...or'**, **'Neither...nor'**, **'Not only...but also'**, or **'Or'**, the verb agrees with the **closest subject (nearest noun/pronoun)**.
• **Rule Mechanism:** Ignore Subject 1; look only at Subject 2 (the noun right before the verb).
• **Mnemonic:** **"NEAREST NEIGHBOR RULE"** → The verb matches the neighbor closest to it.
• **Example 1:** Incorrect: Either Ramesh or his friends **has** stolen the purse. | **Correct:** Either Ramesh or his friends **have** stolen the purse. ('friends' is plural and closer to verb)
• **Example 2:** Incorrect: Neither the students nor the teacher **were** present. | **Correct:** Neither the students nor the teacher **was** present. ('teacher' is singular)
• **Example 3:** Incorrect: Not only the principal but also the teachers **was** protesting. | **Correct:** Not only the principal but also the teachers **were** protesting. ('teachers' is plural)
• **Example 4:** Incorrect: Has Mohan or his brothers **done** this? | **Correct:** **Have** Mohan or his brothers done this? (In interrogative sentences, verb matches nearest subject 'Mohan' → wait, closest subject to verb 'Have' in front is 'Mohan', so **Has Mohan or his brothers done this?**)
• **Example 5:** Incorrect: Neither you nor I **are** to be blamed. | **Correct:** Neither you nor I **am** to be blamed. (Verb matches 'I')

items.title: Rule 3: Intervening Phrases & Parenthetical Expressions (distractor Clause)
items.content:
• **General Rule:** Words joined to a subject by **'as well as'**, **'along with'**, **'together with'**, **'with'**, **'in addition to'**, **'besides'**, **'accompanied by'**, **'like'**, **'unlike'**, **'including'**, **'headed by'** do NOT alter the subject's number.
• **Core Principle:** The verb agrees strictly with the **FIRST SUBJECT**. Ignore everything inside the prepositions/phrases.
• **Mnemonic:** **"IGNORE THE ATTACHMENT"** → Subject 1 + [Connector + Subject 2] + **Verb (matches Subject 1)**
• **Example 1:** Incorrect: The Captain along with his crew members **were** drowned. | **Correct:** The Captain along with his crew members **was** drowned. (Subject 1 = 'Captain' [Singular])
• **Example 2:** Incorrect: The teacher as well as the students **are** going on a tour. | **Correct:** The teacher as well as the students **is** going on a tour. (Subject 1 = 'teacher')
• **Example 3:** Incorrect: The chief with all his soldiers **were** killed in action. | **Correct:** The chief with all his soldiers **was** killed in action.
• **Example 4:** Incorrect: You, besides your brother, **has** failed the test. | **Correct:** You, besides your brother, **have** failed the test. (Subject 1 = 'You')
• **Example 5:** Incorrect: My books, in addition to my laptop, **was** stolen. | **Correct:** My books, in addition to my laptop, **were** stolen. (Subject 1 = 'books')

items.title: Rule 4: Indefinite Pronouns & Quantifiers (अनिश्चित सर्वनाम नियम)
items.content:
• **Always Singular Indefinite Pronouns:** **Each, Every, Everyone, Someone, Somebody, Anyone, Anybody, Nobody, No one, Either (of), Neither (of), One (of), Many a** → Take **SINGULAR VERB**.
• **Always Plural Indefinite Pronouns:** **Both, Few, A few, Several, Many** → Take **PLURAL VERB**.
• **Variable Indefinite Pronouns (SANAM Rule):** **S**ome, **A**ll, **N**one, **A**ny, **M**ost → Singular if Uncountable Noun follows; Plural if Countable Plural Noun follows.
• **Mnemonic:** **"SANAM Rule"** = Look at the noun after **'of'**.
• **Example 1:** Incorrect: Each of the boys **have** submitted their assignment. | **Correct:** Each of the boys **has** submitted his assignment. ('Each' = Singular Verb + Singular Possessive 'his')
• **Example 2:** Incorrect: One of my friends **are** an engineer. | **Correct:** One of my friends **is** an engineer.
• **Example 3:** Incorrect: Many a student **have** failed the PET examination. | **Correct:** Many a student **has** failed the PET examination. ('Many a' + Singular Noun + Singular Verb)
• **Example 4:** Incorrect: Some of the water **were** spilled on the floor. | **Correct:** Some of the water **was** spilled on the floor. (Water = Uncountable → SV)
• **Example 5:** Incorrect: Some of the books **was** damaged. | **Correct:** Some of the books **were** damaged. (Books = Plural Countable → PV)

items.title: Rule 5: Collective Nouns, Quantities, and Nouns Ending in 'S'
items.content:
• **Collective Nouns (Committee, Jury, Team, Class, Audience, Family):** Take **Singular Verb** when acting as a **single unified body**; take **Plural Verb** when members act **individually or are divided**.
• **Amounts / Distance / Time / Weights:** Expressing a single lump sum or total quantity takes a **Singular Verb**.
• **Plural Form - Singular Meaning Nouns:** **News, Physics, Mathematics, Economics, Politics, Ethics, Measles, Rickets, Billiards, Series, Innings** → Take **SINGULAR VERB**.
• **Mnemonic:** **"UNITED = SINGULAR | DIVIDED = PLURAL"**
• **Example 1:** Incorrect: The Jury **were** unanimous in its decision. | **Correct:** The Jury **was** unanimous in its decision. (Unified body)
• **Example 2:** Incorrect: The Jury **was** divided in their opinions. | **Correct:** The Jury **were** divided in their opinions. (Divided individuals)
• **Example 3:** Incorrect: Ten miles **are** a long distance to walk. | **Correct:** Ten miles **is** a long distance to walk. (Single unit of distance)
• **Example 4:** Incorrect: Mathematics **are** a difficult subject for many. | **Correct:** Mathematics **is** a difficult subject for many.
• **Example 5:** Incorrect: Fifty thousand rupees **were** spent on a single watch. | **Correct:** Fifty thousand rupees **was** spent on a single watch. (Lump sum)

sections.title: Comprehensive Rule & Classification Tables
rows: 'A number of' vs 'The number of'

**A number of** + Plural Noun + **Plural Verb**
**The number of** + Plural Noun + **Singular Verb**

• **Incorrect:** A number of students **is** absent today.
• **Correct:** A number of students **are** absent today.
• **Correct:** The number of students in the class **is** 50.
Relative Pronoun Antecedent Rule

Noun + **Who / Which / That** + Verb
*Verb must agree with the Noun (Antecedent) placed immediately BEFORE the relative pronoun.*

• **Incorrect:** It is I who **is** responsible for this error.
• **Correct:** It is I who **am** responsible for this error. (Antecedent = 'I')
• **Correct:** He is one of those men who **always help** others.
Uncountable Nouns (अगणनीय संज्ञाएँ)
Furniture, Advice, Information, Luggage, Baggage, Hair, Knowledge, Scenery, Poetry, Work, Equipment → **Always Singular Verb**

• **Incorrect:** The sceneries of Kashmir **are** breathtaking.
• **Correct:** The scenery of Kashmir **is** breathtaking.
• **Incorrect:** All his informations **were** false.
• **Correct:** All his information **was** false.
Plural Pair Nouns

Scissors, Trousers, Pants, Spectacles, Pliers, Shorts, Binoculars → **Plural Verb**
*If preceded by 'A pair of' → **Singular Verb***

• **Incorrect:** My spectacles **is** broken.
• **Correct:** My spectacles **are** broken.
• **Correct:** A pair of spectacles **has** been purchased.
Fractions and Percentages

**Fraction/Percentage + Uncountable Noun → Singular Verb**
**Fraction/Percentage + Plural Countable Noun → Plural Verb**

• **Correct:** Two-thirds of the work **is** completed.
• **Correct:** Two-thirds of the students **have** passed.
Hypothetical / Unreal Conditions
If / Wish / As if / As though + Subject + **WERE** (Regardess of whether the subject is singular or plural)

• **Incorrect:** If I **was** the Chief Minister, I would help you.
• **Correct:** If I **were** the Chief Minister, I would help you.
• **Correct:** He talks as if he **were** my boss.
'More than' Formulations

1. **More than one** + Singular Noun → **Singular Verb**
2. **More than two/three** → **Plural Verb**
3. **More + Plural Noun + than one** → **Plural Verb**

• **Correct:** More than one boy **was** absent.
• **Correct:** More than two boys **were** absent.
• **Correct:** More boys than one **were** absent.
Cardinal & Nominal Titles
Names of Books, Movies, Novels, Countries, Organizations ending in 'S' → **Singular Verb**

• **Incorrect:** 'Gulliver's Travels' **are** an interesting book.
• **Correct:** 'Gulliver's Travels' **is** an interesting book.
• **Correct:** The United States **has** a strong economy.

items.definition: When you see connecting phrases like **as well as, along with, together with, with, in addition to, besides, except, like, accompanied by**, draw a bracket around everything from the connector to the verb. Match the verb strictly with the **FIRST SUBJECT**. Example: **The King** [along with his soldiers] **was** present.

Remember **A = A Lot = Plural** (**A number of** = Plural Verb). Remember **THE = Specific Singular Total** (**The number of** = Singular Verb). Example: **A number of** workers **have** struck work | **The number of** workers **is** fixed.

**Many** takes a Plural Noun + Plural Verb (**Many students have passed**). But **Many + a/an** MUST take a Singular Noun + Singular Verb (**Many a student HAS passed**). Never put a plural noun after 'Many a'.

For **S**ome, **A**ll, **N**one, **A**ny, **M**ost or Fractions/Percentages: Look at the Noun AFTER 'of'. Noun is Uncountable → **Singular Verb** (**30% of the water IS polluted**). Noun is Plural Countable → **Plural Verb** (**30% of the students ARE present**).

In imaginary, hypothetical, or conditional sentences starting with **If, I wish, Would that, As though**, completely abandon 'was'. Always use **WERE** regardless of whether the subject is I, He, She, It, or They. Example: **I wish I WERE a king** (NOT 'was').

Tools/Garments with two identical parts (Scissors, Trousers, Spectacles, Goggles) are **always Plural** and take a **Plural Verb**. BUT, the moment the phrase **'A pair of'** is added before them, the subject becomes 'pair' (singular) → **Singular Verb**. Example: **Scissors ARE sharp** vs **A pair of scissors IS on the table**.

items.term: Error 1: Error of Proximity (समीपवर्ती संज्ञा का भ्रम)
items.definition: Mistaking the noun immediately preceding the verb for the actual subject. **Incorrect:** The quality of these mangoes **are** not good. **Correct:** The quality of these mangoes **is** not good. (Real Subject = 'Quality', not 'mangoes').

items.term: Error 2: Plural Verb with 'Each of' / 'One of' / 'Neither of'
items.definition: Candidates see a plural noun after 'of' and erroneously use a plural verb. **Incorrect:** Each of the candidates **have** cleared the written exam. **Correct:** Each of the candidates **has** cleared the written exam. ('Each' is the singular subject).

items.term: Error 3: Adding 's/es' to Uncountable Nouns to Make Them Plural
items.definition: Nouns like *Scenery, Furniture, Advice, Luggage, Information, Hair* do NOT have plural forms. **Incorrect:** The furnitures **were** sold. **Correct:** The furniture **was** sold.

items.term: Error 4: Using Singular Verb with 'A Number of'
items.definition: Candidates assume 'A' means singular and select a singular verb. **Incorrect:** A number of issues **was** raised. **Correct:** A number of issues **were** raised.

items.term: Error 5: Misinterpreting Subject in Relative Clauses ('One of the... who')
items.definition: In sentences like 'He is one of the men who work here', the relative pronoun 'who' refers to 'men' (plural), NOT 'one'. **Incorrect:** He is one of those boys who **plays** cricket. **Correct:** He is one of those boys who **play** cricket.

items.term: Error 6: Using Plural Verbs for Academic Subjects and Diseases ending in 'S'
items.definition: Treating words like *Physics, Mathematics, News, Diabetes, Measles* as plural. **Incorrect:** Physics **are** my favorite subject. **Correct:** Physics **is** my favorite subject.
Singular subjects require singular verbs (**is, was, has, V1+s/es**); plural subjects require plural verbs (**are, were, have, V1**).
Two subjects joined by **'and'** take a **Plural Verb**, unless they represent a single unit, meal, or identical person.
With **Either...or / Neither...nor / Not only...but also**, the verb agrees with the **closest noun**.
Phrases like **as well as, along with, together with, with, in addition to** do NOT alter the subject; match the verb to the **first subject**.
**Each, Every, Either, Neither, Everyone, Nobody, One** strictly take **Singular Verbs**.
**'A number of'** takes a **Plural Verb**; **'The number of'** takes a **Singular Verb**.
**'Many a'** is followed by a **Singular Noun** and a **Singular Verb**.
Collective nouns take **Singular Verb** when acting as a unit, and **Plural Verb** when divided or acting individually.
Nouns like **furniture, advice, information, luggage, scenery** always take **Singular Verbs**.
**Scissors, trousers, spectacles** take **Plural Verbs**, but **'A pair of...'** takes a **Singular Verb**.
Unreal conditions starting with **'If' / 'I wish'** always take **'WERE'** regardless of the subject.
The verb after **Who / Which / That** must agree with the **antecedent noun** placed directly before it.

upscNotes.content: UPSSSC PET Exam Strategy: In Spotting Error questions, always locate the main action verb first, put a finger on it, and ask 'WHO or WHAT is doing this action?' to find the true subject. Ignore all prepositional phrases sandwiched in between.

Common MCQ Trap: Examiners often place a plural noun right before the verb (e.g., 'The box of chocolates **are** missing') to trick candidates into choosing a plural verb. Always trace back to the head noun ('box').

Rule of One: Pay special attention to 'One of the + Plural Noun'. While 'One of the students **is** coming' takes a singular verb, 'One of the students who **have** passed' takes a plural verb because of the relative pronoun 'who'.
Possessive & Article Trap: 'The Manager and Accountant **has** come' (One person, single 'The') vs 'The Manager and **the** Accountant **have** come' (Two persons, two 'The's). Count the articles!

keyTakeaways: Singular Subject takes Singular Verb (V1+s/es); Plural Subject takes Plural Verb (V1).
'As well as', 'along with', and 'together with' agree strictly with the FIRST subject.
'Either...or' and 'Neither...nor' agree with the NEAREST subject.
'Each', 'Every', 'Either', 'Neither', and 'Many a' ALWAYS take a Singular Verb.
'A number of' = Plural Verb; 'The number of' = Singular Verb.
Uncountable nouns (Information, Scenery, Advice, Furniture) ALWAYS take a Singular Verb.
Imaginary/Conditional statements (If, I wish) ALWAYS use 'WERE'.

practice.question: Identify the segment in the sentence which contains a grammatical error: 'The teacher along with (A) / his students were present (B) / at the annual function. (C) / No error (D)'
practice.explanation: When two subjects are connected by phrases like 'along with', 'together with', 'as well as', or 'accompanied by', the verb agrees with the FIRST subject ('The teacher', which is singular). Therefore, 'were present' should be replaced with 'was present'.

practice.question: Fill in the blank with the most appropriate option: 'Neither the principal nor the teachers _______ satisfied with the new timetable.'
practice.explanation: When subjects are joined by 'neither... nor' or 'either... or', the verb agrees with the subject closest to it. Here, the closest subject 'teachers' is plural, so the plural verb 'were' is correct.

practice.question: Fill in the blank with the correct form of the verb: 'The number of applicants for the UPSSSC examination _______ increased significantly this year.'
practice.explanation: 'The number of' denotes a definite number and takes a SINGULAR verb (has), whereas 'A number of' takes a PLURAL verb. Hence, 'has' is the correct choice.

practice.question: Select the option that improves the underlined part of the sentence: 'Ramesh is one of those boys who **has always helped** the poor.'
practice.explanation: In sentences using 'one of those [plural noun] who/that/which', the relative pronoun ('who') refers back to the plural noun ('boys'). Therefore, the verb following 'who' must be plural ('have always helped').

practice.question: Find the error in the given sentence: 'Mathematics are (A) / considered a difficult subject (B) / by many competitive exam aspirants. (C) / No error (D)'
practice.explanation: Names of academic subjects, diseases, games, and news (e.g., Mathematics, Physics, Measles, Billiards, News) look plural in form but take a singular verb. 'Mathematics are' should be 'Mathematics is'.

practice.question: Fill in the blank: 'Many a candidate _______ failed to clear the physical test this year.'
practice.explanation: The phrase 'Many a' is always followed by a singular countable noun ('candidate') and a SINGULAR verb ('has').

practice.question: Select the correct option to fill in the blank: 'The jury _______ divided in their opinions regarding the final decision.'
practice.explanation: Collective nouns (like jury, committee, team) take a singular verb when acting as a single unit, but take a PLURAL verb ('were') when the members are divided or acting individually (indicated here by 'their opinions').

practice.question: Improve the underlined portion: 'Each of the participants **have been given** a certificate of appreciation.'
practice.explanation: 'Each of', 'Either of', and 'Neither of' are followed by a plural noun/pronoun, but always take a SINGULAR verb. Thus, 'have been given' should be replaced by 'has been given'.

practice.question: Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error: 'Three-fourths of the work (A) / have already been (B) / completed successfully. (C) / No error (D)'
practice.explanation: When fractions or percentages refer to an uncountable noun ('work'), they take a singular verb. Therefore, 'have already been' should be corrected to 'has already been'.

practice.question: Choose the correct indirect form of the sentence: The officer said, 'Every employee needs to submit their report today.'
options: The officer said that every employee needed to submit their report that day.
The officer said that every employee need to submit their report that day.
The officer said that every employees needed to submit their report today.
The officer told that every employee needs to submit their report that day.
practice.explanation: In indirect speech, the reporting verb is in the past tense ('said'), so 'needs' changes to 'needed'. 'Every employee' takes a singular verb contextually, and 'today' changes to 'that day'.

practice.question: Fill in the blank: 'A pair of spectacles _______ lying on the bedside table.'
practice.explanation: Nouns like 'spectacles', 'scissors', 'trousers' are plural by default, but when preceded by 'a pair of', the subject becomes singular ('a pair'), requiring a singular verb ('is').

practice.question: Identify the error in the sentence: 'There is (A) / many reasons (B) / for his sudden resignation. (C) / No error (D)'
practice.explanation: When a sentence starts with introductory 'There', the verb agrees with the real subject that comes after it. Since 'many reasons' is plural, the correct verb should be 'There are'.

practice.question: Select the correct option to improve the underlined section: 'Not only the manager but also his assistants **was present at** the meeting.'
practice.explanation: With the correlative conjunction 'Not only... but also', the verb agrees with the second subject (the one closer to the verb). Here, 'his assistants' is plural, so 'were present at' is correct.

practice.question: Choose the correct indirect speech form: She said, 'Bread and butter is my daily breakfast.'
options: She said that bread and butter was her daily breakfast.
She said that bread and butter were her daily breakfast.
She says that bread and butter is her daily breakfast.
She told that bread and butter are her daily breakfast.
practice.explanation: 'Bread and butter' refers to a single idea/meal, so it takes a singular verb ('is'). In reported speech with a past reporting verb ('said'), 'is' changes to 'was'.

practice.question: Fill in the blank: 'More than one student _______ absent from the class yesterday.'
practice.explanation: The phrase 'More than one' is grammatically followed by a singular noun ('student') and a SINGULAR verb ('was').

pyqs.question: Fill in the blank with the correct form of the verb: 'The quality of these mangoes _____ not good.'
pyqs.explanation: The true subject of the sentence is the singular noun 'quality', not the plural noun 'mangoes' in the prepositional phrase. Therefore, the singular verb 'is' is used.

pyqs.question: Choose the correct option to fill in the blank: 'Either you or he _____ responsible for this mistake.'
pyqs.explanation: When two subjects are connected by 'either...or', the verb agrees with the subject closest to it. Here, the pronoun closest to the verb is 'he' (singular), so the singular verb 'is' is correct.

pyqs.question: Choose the correct verb form: 'Neither the teacher nor the students _____ present in the classroom.'
pyqs.explanation: When subjects are joined by 'neither...nor', the verb agrees with the subject nearest to it. Since 'students' is plural and closest to the blank, the plural verb 'were' is used.

pyqs.question: Fill in the blank with the appropriate verb: 'Bread and butter _____ his wholesome food.'
pyqs.explanation: When two singular nouns joined by 'and' express a single idea, meal, or combination, they are treated as a single singular subject and take a singular verb ('is').

pyqs.question: Select the correct verb to complete the sentence: 'One of my friends _____ a well-known doctor in Delhi.'
pyqs.explanation: The structure 'One of + plural noun' always takes a singular verb because the real subject is 'One' (singular).

pyqs.question: Choose the correct option: 'Fifty kilometers _____ a long distance to cover on foot.'
pyqs.explanation: Plural nouns representing a single unit of distance, weight, time, or money take a singular verb. Therefore, 'Fifty kilometers' is considered a single unit of distance and takes 'is'.

pyqs.question: Fill in the blank: 'Each of the participants _____ awarded a certificate of appreciation.'
pyqs.explanation: Indefinite pronouns such as 'Each', 'Every', 'Either', and 'Neither' followed by 'of + plural noun' always take a singular verb ('was').

pyqs.question: Fill in the blank with the appropriate option: 'The District Magistrate and Collector _____ on an official visit today.'
pyqs.explanation: When two titles refer to the same person (indicated by the definite article 'The' preceding only the first title), a singular verb ('is') is required.

pyqs.question: Select the correct form of verb: 'The jury _____ divided in their opinions.'
pyqs.explanation: Collective nouns (like jury, committee, team) take a plural verb when the members are acting individually or divided in opinion, as indicated by the pronoun 'their'.

pyqs.question: Fill in the blank with the correct verb: 'Not only the manager but also the workers _____ present at the meeting.'
pyqs.explanation: When subjects are joined by 'Not only...but also', the verb agrees with the subject closest to it. Here, 'workers' is plural, so it requires the plural verb 'were'.

test.question: Choose the correct verb to complete the sentence: 'Neither Rohan nor his friends _____ attending the party tonight.'
test.explanation: When subjects are connected by 'neither... nor', the verb agrees with the subject closest to it. Here, 'his friends' is plural, so 'are' is the correct verb.

test.question: Fill in the blank with the appropriate verb: 'The committee _____ decided to submit its report tomorrow.'
test.explanation: A collective noun takes a singular verb when the group acts as a single unit. The pronoun 'its' indicates a singular collective unit, so 'has' is correct.

test.question: Select the option that correctly completes the sentence: 'The teacher, along with her students, _____ going on a field trip.'
test.explanation: When a subject is joined to another noun using phrases like 'along with', 'as well as', or 'together with', the verb agrees with the primary subject ('The teacher'), which is singular.

test.question: Identify the correct option: 'Mathematics _____ considered a difficult subject by many students.'
test.explanation: Names of subjects (like Mathematics, Physics, Economics) end in 's' but are singular in meaning and take a singular verb ('is').

test.question: Fill in the blank: 'One of my closest friends _____ moving to London next month.'
test.explanation: The phrase 'One of the + plural noun' always takes a singular verb because the subject is 'One', not the plural noun that follows.

test.question: Choose the correct verb: 'A pair of scissors _____ required for the craft project.'
test.explanation: While 'scissors' alone takes a plural verb, when preceded by 'A pair of', it refers to a single object and takes a singular verb ('is').

test.question: Fill in the blank with the suitable verb: 'Each boy and each girl _____ given a prize at the annual function.'
test.explanation: When two singular nouns connected by 'and' are preceded by 'each' or 'every', they take a singular verb ('was').

test.question: Select the correct option to fill in the blank: 'Ten thousand rupees _____ a large sum for a fresh graduate.'
test.explanation: Amounts of money, distances, periods of time, and measurements take a singular verb when considered as a single total quantity.

test.question: Choose the correct verb form: 'Many a student _____ failed to clear the preliminary examination.'
test.explanation: The structure 'Many a + singular noun' always takes a singular verb ('has').

test.question: Fill in the blank: 'Neither of the two proposals _____ acceptable to the board of directors.'
test.explanation: 'Neither' refers to 'not one or the other' and is followed by a singular verb ('is') when used as a pronoun referring to two items.
